## The Setup

Another classic dataset for illustrating the IV concept was introduced by
[Card (1995)](index.qmd#ref-card-1995). It was used to study the impact of (college) education on
wages, using whether an individual lives close to a college as an instrument for (college)
education. An important characteristic of the setup is that the instrument is most likely not
randomly assigned.

We consider a binarized version of the treatment, i.e. an individual is treated if their education
is recorded as at least 13 years. The treatment can therefore be viewed as _some college_.

This is in line with modern takes on the dataset, such as
[Słoczyński (2021)](index.qmd#ref-sloczynski-2021) and
[Tübbicke (2023)](index.qmd#ref-tubbicke-2023). Notice that these papers and the corresponding
packages do not focus on quantile treatment effects.

The dataset consists of 3,010 men from the 1976 National Longitudinal Survey of Young Men. The
instrument `nearc4` indicates whether a man grew up in a local labour market with a four-year
college, and the outcome `lwage` is the log wage.

In @lst-card-sample, we follow [Słoczyński (2021)](index.qmd#ref-sloczynski-2021) and
[Tübbicke (2023)](index.qmd#ref-tubbicke-2023) in restricting the sample to covariate cells with at
least five observations. A cell is one of the observed combinations of `black`, `south66`, `south`,
`smsa66` and `smsa`. This drops 22 observations and leaves 2,988.

```{python}
#| label: lst-card-sample
#| code-summary: "Show code (estimation sample)"
#| code-fold: false
import polars as pl

from qte.datasets import load_card

CARD_CELLS = ["black", "south66", "south", "smsa66", "smsa"]
CARD_COVARIATES = (
    "exper + expersq + black + south + smsa + smsa66 "
    "+ reg662 + reg663 + reg664 + reg665 + reg666 + reg667 + reg668 + reg669"
)

sample = load_card(treatment_cutoff=13)
card = sample.filter(pl.len().over(CARD_CELLS) >= 5)
print(f"{sample.height} observations, {sample.height - card.height} dropped, {card.height} left")
```

## Descriptive Statistics

@lst-card-data shows how to generate descriptive statistics by instrument value, by treatment status
and for the entire dataset with the `make_descriptive_statistics` function from `py-qte`;
@tbl-card-data shows the results.

```{python}
#| label: lst-card-data
#| code-summary: "Show code (Generation of descriptive statistics)"
#| code-fold: false
from qte.iv.descriptives import make_descriptive_statistics

t_desc = make_descriptive_statistics(
    card,
    "lwage",
    "college",
    "nearc4",
    covariates=["exper", "educ", "age", "black", "smsa66", "south66"],
    labels={
        "lwage": "Log wage",
        "college": "College",
        "exper": "Experience",
        "educ": "Years of education",
        "age": "Age",
        "black": "Black",
        "smsa66": "SMSA in 1966",
        "south66": "South in 1966",
    },
    title="Table 1. Card Data, Means and Standard Deviations",
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-card-data
#| code-summary: "Show code (Card descriptive statistics)"
t_desc
```

@tbl-card-data reveals large differences across instrument values for most covariates, and most of
these differences are statistically significant. One can, therefore, not assume that the instrument
is (as good as) randomly assigned, and the analysis should condition any first stage on covariates.

## Unconditional Local QTE

In @lst-card-estimate, we estimate unconditional local treatment effects using the
`estimate_unconditional_local_effects` function from `py-qte`. We use a large number of bootstrap
replications to estimate the standard errors. The result object returned by
`estimate_unconditional_local_effects` carries its own presentation methods: `plot` for the figure
and `tabulate` for the table, both generated in @lst-card-estimate and shown side by side in
@fig-card-plot.

Notice that we use `Estimator.SIGNED` as the estimation method here which computes the empirical cdf
directly from Abadie's kappa weights.

```{python}
#| label: lst-card-estimate
#| code-summary: "Show code (local QTE on the Card data)"
#| code-fold: false
QUANTILES = [0.10, 0.50, 0.90]

with timer("card"):
    card_res = estimate_unconditional_local_effects(
        card,
        "lwage",
        "college",
        "nearc4",
        qs=QUANTILES,
        instrument_probability_formula=CARD_COVARIATES,
        estimator=Estimator.SIGNED,
        bootstrap_config=BootstrapConfig(n_iter=1000, seed=42, n_workers=4),
    )

card_fig = card_res.plot()
card_tbl = card_res.tabulate(quantiles=QUANTILES)
```

@fig-card-plot reports the results.

```{python}
#| label: fig-card-plot
#| code-summary: "Show code (plot and table side by side)"
#| fig-cap: "Local quantile treatment effects on the Card data."
import vl_convert as vlc
from IPython.display import publish_display_data

plot_svg = vlc.vegalite_to_svg(card_fig.to_dict())
table_html = card_tbl.as_raw_html()
publish_display_data(
    {"text/html": f'<div class="iv-side"><div>{plot_svg}</div><div>{table_html}</div></div>'}
)
```

For the mean, the results are close to those reported by
[Tübbicke (2023)](index.qmd#ref-tubbicke-2023), both in point estimates and in standard errors. For
compliers, some college education raises income by about 35% (0.309 log points), and this effect is
quite imprecisely measured. The point estimate is larger than the OLS estimate of about 0.24 log
points, but much smaller than the 2SLS estimate of about 0.60 log points that Tübbicke (2023)
reports; the latter implies a hard-to-believe return of roughly 80%. The results also suggest that
there is little effect heterogeneity across the quantiles.
